description: We're a team of students passionate about aerospace engineering and space science. We came to the Space Apps Challenge to take on real NASA problems and turn open data into something useful.
summary:
In space there is no fire department to call, so fire safety has to be designed in before launch, and fire behaves differently without gravity.

EmberAtlas is the firefighter for space: a web simulator that shows habitat designers how a cabin fire would start and spread, and how to stop it before anything flies.

- Build with AI: describe a cabin in plain English, and AI drafts the scenario from a material library, leaving unsourced inputs blank rather than guessing.
- 3D fire simulation: a physics engine calibrated on 18 NASA ISS fire experiments (2,818 data rows) burns the cabin, runs it 200 times for uncertainty bands, and compares conditions side by side, such as the ISS vs a Moon base.
- Ask Aster: our AI fire engineer explains results with NASA citations, and every number it quotes is checked against the engine.
- Design fixes: ranked changes, plus the next NASA experiment that would close the biggest evidence gap.
- Evidence trail: every number traces to its NASA file and row, and results beyond NASA's tested range are labelled as extrapolated.

As crews head to the Moon and beyond, EmberAtlas turns scattered NASA research into fire-safety decisions engineers can act on.
details:
Designers of lunar and orbital habitats must judge fire risk for cabins that have never been built, using experimental data collected under very different conditions. EmberAtlas closes that gap. It is a web simulator that shows where a fire would start in a spacecraft or habitat, how it would spread, and which design change would prevent it. It is built on NASA's ISS combustion data and uses AI to explain the results.

HOW IT WORKS: FIVE STEPS

1. Describe: a user describes a cabin in plain English. AI drafts a scenario from a material library and leaves any unsourced field blank for the user rather than guessing.

2. Simulate: a calibrated engine models a well-mixed cabin with a flame front for each item, and runs each scenario 200 times (Monte Carlo) to produce uncertainty bands.

3. Visualize: the fire plays out in a 3D cabin, with a timeline and charts for heat, oxygen, CO2 and smoke.

4. Explain: Aster, our AI fire engineer, answers questions about the run and NASA research. It may only use engine output and cited NASA experiments, and every number it quotes is checked against the simulation.

5. Fix: EmberAtlas ranks design changes and proposes the next NASA experiment that would close the biggest gap in the evidence.

WHAT IT SHOWS

In the Moon-base example (34% oxygen, 56.5 kPa, lunar gravity), the same fire that goes out in 30 seconds on the ISS burns for 171 seconds, about 5.7 times longer, and the site labels that result as extrapolated. The highest oxygen level at which NASA tested any solid is 22.2%, so the Moon-base atmosphere sits about 12 points beyond the tested range, and the tool says so. Its suggested fixes include giving the alarm a way to trigger, testing the fabric at 34% oxygen, and lowering cabin oxygen to 29.2%, which reduces modelled peak heat from 4,920 W to 4,040 W. Instead of only reporting a risk, EmberAtlas points to a design change and the experiment that would test it.

CREATIVITY

Much of the creativity is in how the system limits itself. The AI cannot invent numbers, missing inputs are never guessed, and every result carries an evidence label: NASA-measured, calibrated, or extrapolated. Presets such as "ISS vs Moon base" and "Saffire-III replay" give users an easy way in. We designed for a realistic user: Maya, a fictional lunar-habitat fire-safety engineer. The interface is available in seven languages: English, French, Spanish, Portuguese, Chinese, Hindi and Tamil.

NASA DATA

The foundation is the NASA Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) repository: 18 ISS fire experiments and 2,818 data rows, each traced to its NASA file and row. We also use NASA technical reports on Saffire, BASS-II, FLEX, lunar-gravity flammability (FM2, LUCI) and the 34% O2 exploration atmosphere.

HONEST ABOUT ITS LIMITS

Our extracted data matches NASA's published tables with zero mismatches across 1,533 checked values. Model accuracy is reported openly: 5 of 16 validation targets pass, droplet burning-rate error is 13.3% across 66 held-out NASA tests, and flame-spread error for SIBAL fabric is 29.3% (based on a single case). Partial-gravity results are estimates that may be non-conservative, the smoke model is uncalibrated, and the tool is not for flight certification. The Methods page documents all of it.

TOOLS AND LANGUAGES

TypeScript, React 19 and Next.js 15 (web app); Tailwind CSS; Three.js with React Three Fiber (3D cabin); Python with NumPy, SciPy, pandas and scikit-learn (physics engine and data pipeline, ported to TypeScript for the browser); the OpenAI API (Aster and the scenario builder); Vitest and Playwright (testing); Vercel (hosting); GitHub (source code, with a "Use of AI" section).

IMPACT

EmberAtlas helps designers find fire risks, and the next test worth running, before hardware flies. As crews travel to the Moon and beyond, early and transparent guidance like this makes safer habitats easier to design.
